</div><div class="mw-content-ltr mw-parser-output" lang="en" dir="ltr"><div class="shortdescription nomobile noexcerpt noprint searchaux" style="display:none">Computer authentication protocol</div>

   / 30 January 2026<span class="noprint">&#59;&#32;4 months ago</span><span style="display:none">&#160;(<span class="bday dtstart published updated">30 January 2026</span>)</span></div></td></tr><tr style="display:none"><td colspan="2">
</td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="infobox-label" style="white-space: nowrap;">Written in</th><td class="infobox-data"><a href="/wiki/C_(programming_language)" title="C (programming language)">C</a></td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="infobox-label" style="white-space: nowrap;"><a href="/wiki/Operating_system" title="Operating system">Operating system</a></th><td class="infobox-data"><a href="/wiki/Cross-platform" class="mw-redirect" title="Cross-platform">Cross-platform</a></td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="infobox-label" style="white-space: nowrap;"><a href="/wiki/Software_categories#Categorization_approaches" title="Software categories">Type</a></th><td class="infobox-data"><a href="/wiki/Authentication_protocol" title="Authentication protocol">Authentication protocol</a></td></tr><tr><th scope="row" class="infobox-label" style="white-space: nowrap;">Website</th><td class="infobox-data"><span class="url"><a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://web.mit.edu/kerberos/">web<wbr />.mit<wbr />.edu<wbr />/kerberos<wbr />/</a></span></td></tr></tbody></table> 
<p><b>Kerberos</b> (<span class="rt-commentedText nowrap"><span class="IPA nopopups noexcerpt" lang="en-fonipa"><a href="/wiki/Help:IPA/English" title="Help:IPA/English">/<span style="border-bottom:1px dotted"><span title="/ˈ/: primary stress follows">ˈ</span><span title="&#39;k&#39; in &#39;kind&#39;">k</span><span title="/ɜːr/: &#39;ur&#39; in &#39;fur&#39;">ɜːr</span><span title="&#39;b&#39; in &#39;buy&#39;">b</span><span title="/ər/: &#39;er&#39; in &#39;letter&#39;">ər</span><span title="/ɒ/: &#39;o&#39; in &#39;body&#39;">ɒ</span><span title="&#39;s&#39; in &#39;sigh&#39;">s</span></span>/</a></span></span>) is a <a href="/wiki/Computer_network" title="Computer network">computer-network</a> <a href="/wiki/Authentication" title="Authentication">authentication</a> <a href="/wiki/Cryptographic_protocol" title="Cryptographic protocol">protocol</a> that works on the basis of <i>tickets</i> to allow <a href="/wiki/Node_(networking)" title="Node (networking)">nodes</a> communicating over a non-secure network to prove their identity to one another in a secure manner. Its designers aimed it primarily at a <a href="/wiki/Client%E2%80%93server" class="mw-redirect" title="Client–server">client–server</a> model, and it provides <a href="/wiki/Mutual_authentication" title="Mutual authentication">mutual authentication</a>—both the user and the server verify each other's identity. Kerberos protocol messages are protected against <a href="/wiki/Computer_insecurity#Eavesdropping" class="mw-redirect" title="Computer insecurity">eavesdropping</a> and <a href="/wiki/Replay_attack" title="Replay attack">replay attacks</a>.
</p><p>Kerberos builds on <a href="/wiki/Symmetric-key_cryptography" class="mw-redirect" title="Symmetric-key cryptography">symmetric-key cryptography</a> and requires a <a href="/wiki/Trusted_third_party" title="Trusted third party">trusted third party</a>, and optionally may use <a href="/wiki/Public-key_cryptography" title="Public-key cryptography">public-key cryptography</a> during certain phases of authentication.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-rfc4556&#95;2-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-rfc4556-2"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>2<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Kerberos uses <a href="/wiki/UDP_port" class="mw-redirect" title="UDP port">UDP port</a> 88 by default.
</p><p>The protocol was named after the character <i><a href="/wiki/Cerberus" title="Cerberus">Cerberus</a></i>, also spelled <i>Kerberos</i>, from <a href="/wiki/Greek_mythology" title="Greek mythology">Greek mythology</a>, the ferocious three-headed guard dog of <a href="/wiki/Hades" title="Hades">Hades</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-3" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-3"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>3<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
<meta property="mw:PageProp/toc" />
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="History_and_development">History and development</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Kerberos_(protocol)&amp;action=edit&amp;section=1" title="Edit section: History and development"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology" title="Massachusetts Institute of Technology">Massachusetts Institute of Technology</a> (MIT) developed Kerberos in 1988 to protect network services provided by <a href="/wiki/Project_Athena" title="Project Athena">Project Athena</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-FOOTNOTEGarman20035&#95;4-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGarman20035-4"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>4<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-Athena&#95;Network&#95;Services&#95;5-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Athena_Network_Services-5"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>5<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Its first version was primarily designed by Steve Miller and Clifford Neuman based on the earlier <a href="/wiki/Needham%E2%80%93Schroeder_protocol" title="Needham–Schroeder protocol">Needham–Schroeder symmetric-key protocol</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-6" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-6"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>6<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-Building&#95;Internet&#95;Firewalls&#95;7-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-Building_Internet_Firewalls-7"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>7<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Kerberos versions 1 through 3 were experimental and not released outside of MIT.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-FOOTNOTEGarman20037&#95;8-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGarman20037-8"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Kerberos version 4, the first public version, was released on January 24, 1989. Since Kerberos 4 was developed in the United States, and since it used the <a href="/wiki/Data_Encryption_Standard" title="Data Encryption Standard">Data Encryption Standard</a> (DES) <a href="/wiki/Encryption_algorithm" class="mw-redirect" title="Encryption algorithm">encryption</a> algorithm, <a href="/wiki/Export_of_cryptography_from_the_United_States" title="Export of cryptography from the United States">U.S. export control restrictions</a> prevented it from being exported to other countries. MIT created an exportable version of Kerberos 4 with all encryption code removed,<sup id="cite&#95;ref-FOOTNOTEGarman20037&#95;8-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGarman20037-8"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>8<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> called "Bones".<sup id="cite&#95;ref-FOOTNOTEPröhlKobras20227&#95;9-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPröhlKobras20227-9"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>9<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Eric Young of Australia's <a href="/wiki/Bond_University" title="Bond University">Bond University</a> reimplemented DES into Bones, in a version called "eBones", which could be freely used in any country. Sweden's <a href="/wiki/Royal_Institute_of_Technology" class="mw-redirect" title="Royal Institute of Technology">Royal Institute of Technology</a> released another reimplementation called KTH-KRB.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-FOOTNOTEGarman20037–8&#95;10-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGarman20037–8-10"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>10<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Neuman and John Kohl published version 5 in 1993 with the intention of overcoming existing limitations and security problems.  Version&#160;5 appeared as <a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="http://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc1510">RFC&#160;1510</a>, which was then made obsolete by <a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="http://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc4120">RFC&#160;4120</a> in 2005.
</p><p>In 2005, the <a href="/wiki/Internet_Engineering_Task_Force" title="Internet Engineering Task Force">Internet Engineering Task Force</a> (IETF) Kerberos working group updated specifications. Updates included:
</p>
<ul><li>Encryption and Checksum Specifications (<a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="http://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc3961">RFC&#160;3961</a>).</li>
<li><a href="/wiki/Advanced_Encryption_Standard" title="Advanced Encryption Standard">Advanced Encryption Standard</a> (AES) Encryption for Kerberos 5 (<a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="http://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc3962">RFC&#160;3962</a>).</li>
<li>A new edition of the Kerberos V5 specification "The Kerberos Network Authentication Service (V5)" (<a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="http://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc4120">RFC&#160;4120</a>). This version obsoletes RFC&#160;1510, clarifies aspects of the protocol and intended use in a more detailed and clearer explanation.</li>
<li>A new edition of the <a href="/wiki/Generic_Security_Services_Application_Program_Interface" class="mw-redirect" title="Generic Security Services Application Program Interface">Generic Security Services Application Program Interface</a> (GSS-API) specification "The Kerberos Version&#160;5 Generic Security Service Application Program Interface (GSS-API) Mechanism: Version&#160;2" (<a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="http://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc4121">RFC&#160;4121</a>).</li></ul>
<p>MIT makes an implementation of Kerberos freely available, under copyright permissions similar to those used for <a href="/wiki/BSD_licenses" title="BSD licenses">BSD</a>. In 2007, MIT formed the Kerberos Consortium to foster continued development. Founding sponsors include vendors such as <a href="/wiki/Oracle_Corporation" title="Oracle Corporation">Oracle</a>, <a href="/wiki/Apple_Inc." title="Apple Inc.">Apple Inc.</a>, <a href="/wiki/Google" title="Google">Google</a>, <a href="/wiki/Microsoft" title="Microsoft">Microsoft</a>, Centrify Corporation and TeamF1 Inc., and academic institutions such as the <a href="/wiki/Royal_Institute_of_Technology" class="mw-redirect" title="Royal Institute of Technology">Royal Institute of Technology</a> in Sweden, Stanford University, MIT, and vendors such as CyberSafe offering commercially supported versions.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Protocol">Protocol</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Kerberos_(protocol)&amp;action=edit&amp;section=2" title="Edit section: Protocol"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Description">Description</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Kerberos_(protocol)&amp;action=edit&amp;section=3" title="Edit section: Description"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>The client authenticates itself to the <b>Authentication Server (AS)</b> which is part of the <b><a href="/wiki/Key_distribution_center" title="Key distribution center">key distribution center</a></b> <b>(KDC)</b>. The KDC issues a <b>ticket-granting ticket (TGT)</b>, which is time stamped and encrypts it using the <b>ticket-granting service's (TGS)</b> secret key and returns the encrypted result to the user's workstation.  This is done infrequently, typically at user logon; the TGT expires at some point although it may be transparently renewed by the user's session manager while they are logged in.
</p><p>When the client needs to communicate with a service on another node (a "principal", in Kerberos parlance), the client sends the TGT to the TGS, which is another component of the KDC and usually shares the same host as the authentication server. The service must have already been registered with the TGS with a <b>Service Principal Name (SPN)</b>. The client uses the SPN to request access to this service. After verifying that the TGT is valid and that the user is permitted to access the requested service, the TGS issues a <b>service ticket (ST)</b> and session keys to the client. The client then sends the ticket to the <b>service server (SS)</b> along with its service request.
</p>
<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb"><a href="/wiki/File:Kerberos_protocol.svg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Kerberos_protocol.svg/500px-Kerberos_protocol.svg.png" decoding="async" width="380" height="401" style="--mw-file-upright: 1.5" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Kerberos_protocol.svg/960px-Kerberos_protocol.svg.png 2x" data-file-width="645" data-file-height="680" /></a><figcaption>Kerberos negotiations</figcaption></figure>
<p>The protocol is described in detail below.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="User_Client-based_Login_without_Kerberos">User Client-based Login without Kerberos</h4><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Kerberos_(protocol)&amp;action=edit&amp;section=4" title="Edit section: User Client-based Login without Kerberos"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<ol><li>A user enters a username and password on the <a href="/wiki/Client_(computing)" title="Client (computing)">client machine(s)</a>.  Other credential mechanisms like pkinit (RFC 4556) allow for the use of public keys in place of a password. The client transforms the password into the key of a symmetric cipher.  This either uses the built-in <a href="/wiki/Key_scheduling" class="mw-redirect" title="Key scheduling">key scheduling</a>, or a <a href="/wiki/One-way_hash" class="mw-redirect" title="One-way hash">one-way hash</a>, depending on the <a href="/wiki/Cipher_suite" title="Cipher suite">cipher-suite</a> used.</li>
<li>The server receives the username and symmetric cipher and compares it with the data from the database. Login was a success if the cipher matches the cipher that is stored for the user.</li></ol>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="Client_Authentication">Client Authentication</h4><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Kerberos_(protocol)&amp;action=edit&amp;section=5" title="Edit section: Client Authentication"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<ol><li>The client sends a <a href="/wiki/Plaintext" title="Plaintext">plaintext</a> message of the user ID to the AS (Authentication Server) requesting services on behalf of the user. (Note: Neither the secret key nor the password is sent to the AS.)</li>
<li>The AS checks to see whether the client is in its database. If it is, the AS generates the secret key by hashing the password of the user found at the database (e.g., <a href="/wiki/Active_Directory" title="Active Directory">Active Directory</a> in Windows Server) and sends back the following two messages to the client:
<ul><li>Message A: <i>Client/TGS Session Key</i> encrypted using the secret key of the client/user.</li>
<li>Message B: <i>Ticket-Granting-Ticket</i> (TGT, which includes the client ID, client <a href="/wiki/Network_address" title="Network address">network address</a>, ticket validity period, and the <i>Client/TGS Session Key</i>) encrypted using the secret key of the TGS.</li></ul></li>
<li>Once the client receives messages A and B, it attempts to decrypt message A with the secret key generated from the password entered by the user.  If the user entered password does not match the password in the AS database, the client's secret key will be different and thus unable to decrypt message A.  With a valid password and secret key the client decrypts message A to obtain the <i>Client/TGS Session Key</i>. This session key is used for further communications with the TGS. (Note: The client cannot decrypt Message B, as it is encrypted using TGS's secret key.)  At this point, the client has enough information to authenticate itself to the TGS.</li></ol>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="Client_Service_Authorization">Client Service Authorization</h4><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Kerberos_(protocol)&amp;action=edit&amp;section=6" title="Edit section: Client Service Authorization"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<ol><li>When requesting services, the client sends the following messages to the TGS:
<ul><li>Message C: Composed of the message B (the encrypted TGT using the TGS secret key) and the ID of the requested service.</li>
<li>Message D: Authenticator (which is composed of the client ID and the timestamp), encrypted using the <i>Client/TGS Session Key</i> (found by the client in Message A).</li></ul></li>
<li>Upon receiving messages C and D, the TGS retrieves message B out of message C. It decrypts message B using the TGS secret key. This gives it the <i>Client/TGS Session Key</i> and the client ID (both are in the TGT). Using this <i>Client/TGS Session Key</i>, the TGS decrypts message D (Authenticator) and compares the client IDs from messages B and D; if they match, the server sends the following two messages to the client:
<ul><li>Message E: <i>Client-to-server ticket</i> (which includes the client ID, client network address, validity period, and <i>Client/Server Session Key</i>) encrypted using the service's secret key.</li>
<li>Message F: <i>Client/Server Session Key</i> encrypted with the <i>Client/TGS Session Key</i>.</li></ul></li></ol>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading4"><h4 id="Client_Service_Request">Client Service Request</h4><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Kerberos_(protocol)&amp;action=edit&amp;section=7" title="Edit section: Client Service Request"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<ol><li>Upon receiving messages E and F from TGS, the client has enough information to authenticate itself to the Service Server (SS).  The client connects to the SS and sends the following two messages:
<ul><li>Message E: From the previous step (the <i>Client-to-server ticket</i>, encrypted using service's Secret key by the TGS).</li>
<li>Message G: A new Authenticator, which includes the client ID, timestamp and is encrypted using <i>Client/Server Session Key</i>.</li></ul></li>
<li>The SS decrypts the ticket (message E) using its own secret key to retrieve the <i>Client/Server Session Key</i>. Using the sessions key, SS decrypts the Authenticator and compares client ID from messages E and G, if they match server sends the following message to the client to confirm its true identity and willingness to serve the client:
<ul><li>Message H: The timestamp found in client's Authenticator (plus 1 in version 4, but not necessary in version 5<sup id="cite&#95;ref-11" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-11"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>11<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-12" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-12"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>12<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>), encrypted using the <i>Client/Server Session Key</i>.</li></ul></li>
<li>The client decrypts the confirmation (message H) using the <i>Client/Server Session Key</i> and checks whether the timestamp is correct. If so, then the client can trust the server and can start issuing service requests to the server.</li>
<li>The server provides the requested services to the client.</li></ol>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Support_by_operating_systems">Support by operating systems</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Kerberos_(protocol)&amp;action=edit&amp;section=8" title="Edit section: Support by operating systems"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Microsoft_Windows">Microsoft Windows</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Kerberos_(protocol)&amp;action=edit&amp;section=9" title="Edit section: Microsoft Windows"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p><a href="/wiki/Windows_2000" title="Windows 2000">Windows 2000</a> and later versions use Kerberos as their default authentication method.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-MSTN-Kerberos-Auth&#95;13-0" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-MSTN-Kerberos-Auth-13"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>13<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Some <a href="/wiki/Microsoft" title="Microsoft">Microsoft</a> additions to the Kerberos suite of protocols are documented in RFC 3244 "Microsoft Windows 2000 Kerberos Change Password and Set Password Protocols". RFC 4757 documents Microsoft's use of the <a href="/wiki/RC4" title="RC4">RC4</a> cipher.  While Microsoft uses and extends the Kerberos protocol, it does not use the MIT software.
</p><p>Kerberos is used as the preferred authentication method: in general, joining a client to a Windows domain means enabling Kerberos as the default protocol for authentications from that client to services in the Windows domain and all domains with trust relationships to that domain.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-MSTN-Kerberos-Auth&#95;13-1" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-MSTN-Kerberos-Auth-13"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>13<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>In contrast, when either client or server or both are not joined to a domain (or not part of the same trusted domain environment), Windows will instead use <a href="/wiki/NTLM" title="NTLM">NTLM</a> for authentication between client and server.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-MSTN-Kerberos-Auth&#95;13-2" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-MSTN-Kerberos-Auth-13"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>13<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p><p>Internet web applications can enforce Kerberos as an authentication method for domain-joined clients by using APIs provided under <a href="/wiki/SSPI" class="mw-redirect" title="SSPI">SSPI</a>.
</p><p>Microsoft Windows and Windows Server include <style data-mw-deduplicate="TemplateStyles:r886049734">.mw-parser-output .monospaced{font-family:monospace,monospace}</style><span class="monospaced">setspn</span>, a <a href="/wiki/Command-line_interface" title="Command-line interface">command-line</a> utility that can be used to read, modify, or delete the Service Principal Names (SPN) for an Active Directory <a href="/wiki/Service_account" title="Service account">service account</a>.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-14" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-14"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>14<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup><sup id="cite&#95;ref-15" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-15"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>15<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup>
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading3"><h3 id="Unix_and_other_operating_systems">Unix and other operating systems</h3><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Kerberos_(protocol)&amp;action=edit&amp;section=10" title="Edit section: Unix and other operating systems"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>Many Unix-like operating systems, including <a href="/wiki/FreeBSD" title="FreeBSD">FreeBSD</a>, Apple's <a href="/wiki/MacOS" title="MacOS">macOS</a>, <a href="/wiki/Red_Hat_Enterprise_Linux" title="Red Hat Enterprise Linux">Red Hat Enterprise Linux</a>, <a href="/wiki/Sun_microsystems" class="mw-redirect" title="Sun microsystems">Oracle</a>'s <a href="/wiki/Solaris_(operating_system)" class="mw-redirect" title="Solaris (operating system)">Solaris</a>, IBM's <a href="/wiki/AIX" class="mw-redirect" title="AIX">AIX</a>, <a href="/wiki/HP-UX" title="HP-UX">HP-UX</a> and others, include software for Kerberos authentication of users or services. A variety of non-Unix like operating systems such as <a href="/wiki/Z/OS" title="Z/OS">z/OS</a>, <a href="/wiki/IBM_i" title="IBM i">IBM i</a> and <a href="/wiki/OpenVMS" title="OpenVMS">OpenVMS</a> also feature Kerberos support. Embedded implementation of the Kerberos V authentication protocol for client agents and network services running on embedded platforms is also available from companies<sup class="noprint Inline-Template" style="white-space:nowrap;">&#91;<i><a href="/wiki/Wikipedia:Avoid_weasel_words" class="mw-redirect" title="Wikipedia:Avoid weasel words"><span title="The material near this tag possibly uses too vague attribution or weasel words. (November 2023)">which?</span></a></i>&#93;</sup>.
</p>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Drawbacks_and_limitations">Drawbacks and limitations</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Kerberos_(protocol)&amp;action=edit&amp;section=11" title="Edit section: Drawbacks and limitations"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<ul><li>Kerberos has strict time requirements, which means that the clocks of the involved hosts must be synchronized within configured limits. The tickets have a time availability period, and if the host clock is not synchronized with the Kerberos server clock, the authentication will fail. The default configuration <a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="http://web.mit.edu/Kerberos/krb5-1.5/krb5-1.5.4/doc/krb5-admin/Clock-Skew.html">per MIT</a> requires that clock times be no more than five minutes apart. In practice, <a href="/wiki/Network_Time_Protocol" title="Network Time Protocol">Network Time Protocol</a> daemons are usually used to keep the host clocks synchronized. Note that some servers (Microsoft's implementation being one of them) may return a KRB_AP_ERR_SKEW result containing the encrypted server time if both clocks have an offset greater than the configured maximum value. In that case, the client could retry by calculating the time using the provided server time to find the offset. This behavior is documented in <a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="http://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc4430">RFC&#160;4430</a>.</li>
<li>The administration protocol is not standardized and differs between server implementations. Password changes are described in <a rel="nofollow" class="external text" href="https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3244.html">RFC&#160;3244</a>.</li>
<li>In case of symmetric cryptography adoption (Kerberos can work using symmetric or asymmetric (public-key) cryptography), since all authentications are controlled by a centralized <a href="/wiki/Key_distribution_center" title="Key distribution center">key distribution center</a> (KDC), compromise of this authentication infrastructure will allow an attacker to impersonate any user.</li>
<li>Each network service that requires a different host name will need its own set of Kerberos keys. This complicates virtual hosting and clusters.</li>
<li>Kerberos requires user accounts and services to have a trusted relationship to the Kerberos token server.</li>
<li>The required client trust makes creating staged environments (e.g., separate domains for test environment, pre-production environment and production environment) difficult: Either domain trust relationships need to be created that prevent a strict separation of environment domains, or additional user clients need to be provided for each environment.</li></ul>
<div class="mw-heading mw-heading2"><h2 id="Security">Security</h2><span class="mw-editsection"><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">[</span><a href="/w/index.php?title=Kerberos_(protocol)&amp;action=edit&amp;section=12" title="Edit section: Security"><span>edit</span></a><span class="mw-editsection-bracket">]</span></span></div>
<p>The <a href="/wiki/Data_Encryption_Standard" title="Data Encryption Standard">Data Encryption Standard</a> (DES) cipher can be used in combination with Kerberos, but is no longer an Internet standard because it is weak.<sup id="cite&#95;ref-16" class="reference"><a href="#cite_note-16"><span class="cite-bracket">&#91;</span>16<span class="cite-bracket">&#93;</span></a></sup> Security vulnerabilities exist in products that implement legacy versions of Kerberos which lack support for newer encryption ciphers like AES.
</p>
